Great revenue & operating income projections for $ONDS looking ahead to 2027 and beyond (Peter’s post below).

$ONDS (stock) has no doubt struggled this year, along with every other high beta name - without exception.

But I believe the underlying business is fundamentally better positioned than the vast majority of other high beta names out there.

People have lots of opinions about $ONDS’s management and whether or not they’re executing. For me, it’s hard to say they’re not doing a great job in such a small amount of time.

12-18 months ago they were a small wireless communications company that had just announced a bold plan to evolve into a major defense tech firm, and had just begun acquiring the companies needed to do so.

Already, that acquisition spree has been proven largely successful and half a dozen of their new subsidiaries are showing fantastic organic growth rates.

Retail investors are incredibly impatient, however, so when the entire defense sector fell dramatically this year (along with space, quantum, rare earths, nuclear, solar, robotics, etc… and finally AI), criticisms have been rampant across FinX.

I suppose Eric & team should have evolved into a successful defense prime that was growing revenues in the triple digits (or more) and became EBITDA positive in a single year instead of the projected ~2 years.

In the grand scheme of things, this is ridiculous.

Investing can’t, and won’t, always be fast money, all the time.

The stock going the wrong way for most of this year sucks, 100%. But in my opinion, the thesis has only grown stronger.

This is almost exactly what played out for me when I began investing in $RKLB.

I began buying around $15 in 2021 and the stock tanked and stayed in the low to mid single digits for YEARS. The entire time, however, the bull case around the company only got stronger and stronger.

It became laughable at some point how easy it was to spot $RKLB’s current and future success. They had something special and were killing it in the space industry.

Not long after, the stock absolutely mooned and has only come back down (to a mere 1000% gain from 2024 levels) in recent months.

I feel like I’m watching something similar happen in real time with $ONDS.

I’m confident that eventually I’ll be metaphorically looking around the room like, ‘are you kidding me with these share prices??’ the same way I was with $RKLB before the stock exploded.

I’m basically already doing that.

It’s important to note that these are very different companies with completely different business models, but I compare the two here just to express my own feelings and experience around instances where an individual can see potential, or feel confident, in a name that Wall Street (and even other retail investors) think is a dud, or not worth investing in - yet.

(Institutional ownership of $ONDS being at ATHs not withstanding)

Another thing worth saying - I’m content to put almost every stock I come across into the “too hard” pile.

There’s a reason I never invested in fan favorites like $NBIS. The debt structuring, the business model… if I spent a couple hours doing due diligence I’m sure it’d seem like a strong prospect to me, but there’s enough floating around on the surface to make me say, ‘eh, not sure I get it,’ so I just move on.

Names like $RKLB and $ONDS have slapped me in the face with what I see as the obviousness of their impending success.

Names like that are rare for me, so I’m content to buy slowly over years and hold for even longer.

Investing like that isn’t for everyone, and that’s fine. But it’s worth knowing the investment styles of those you follow to ensure you align with them if you’re going to adopt their ideas and follow their trades.

I believe the future is very bright for $ONDS and that the pullback we’re seeing this year is a good opportunity for long-term investors to add.

Please don’t consider this investment advice. This post just outlines my own thoughts and opinions.

Very bad advice: PEG is a tool for steady compounders. For cyclicals, you look at where you are in the cycle—normalized/mid-cycle earnings, price-to-book, capacity, inventory, spreads—not a growth multiple that flatters the peak and punishes the trough. Using PEG on a cyclical is like judging a rollercoaster by its average height: technically true, practically useless.  PEG doesn't work for cyclicals because it assumes earnings growth is smooth and predictable—cyclical earnings are neither.
 
Here's the simple version:
• PEG = P/E ÷ growth rate. It's designed for companies whose earnings grow steadily year after year (like software or consumer staples). A low PEG is supposed to mean "cheap growth."
• Cyclical earnings swing wildly—autos, steel, airlines, semis, energy. In a boom, earnings spike and the P/E looks low. In a bust, earnings collapse and the P/E looks high (or goes negative).
• So PEG gets it backwards. At the top of the cycle, when the stock is actually most dangerous, trailing growth looks great and PEG looks cheap. At the bottom, when the stock may be cheapest, earnings are troughing, growth looks terrible, and PEG looks expensive—or meaningless.
• The "G" is unreliable. A cyclical's growth rate over the past few years tells you almost nothing about the next few, because it's driven by the cycle, not by a durable compounding engine. You're dividing by a number that's about to reverse.

What did we just see with Riemann and what does it mean?  And why isn‘t it immediately rescuing the market?

A meditation on how many here are misunderstanding both the nature of and the implications of the Riemann results.

A key fact about the brilliant Riemann results that many people here are missing: AI *alone* did not solve the Reimann hypothesis. 

Instead an exceptionally talented mathematician with expertise in AI worked together with AI to jointly solve RH.  

As AI math pioneer @ChrSzegedy put, it “Levent made all the right (life) choices at the right time” in order to achieve the result, and we wouldn’t be here others. He didn’t just type in a prompt “Solve Riemann” and get the answer.

Fundamentally, rather, a brilliant mathematician with brilliant instanct drove the process. It took months and a lot of iteration.

And he relied on a special set of resources (see below) that you won’t did for example in medicine.

What actually happened is still super impressive — but it is not what thousands of people seem to believe, and it doesn’t have the same implications.

It does not mean for example that AGI has arrived, or anything like that. (If it had, you wouldn’t have needed the human mathematician to guide the whole process.) 

The other thing that a lot of people aren’t getting is that the RH solution depended on a special-purpose symbolic AI solver with 16 millions of lines of code - built over multiple years by perhaps hundreds  of people — for a specific purpose that is of relatively little value for solving more open-end problems in domains like biology, business, or robotics.  (As I predicted in 2024, verifiable methods have help more with math than other domains.)

Or as @jeremyakahn just put it “Solving RH doesn’t help you negotiate a contract better or correctly figure out a corporate tax return. So no real change to enterprise value prop.”  As @sebkrier put, “Solving an old pure math problem does not immediately widen Anthropic's operating margins"

It’s kind of like what we saw when DeepBlue beat @Kasparov63 in chess in 1997; an absolutely amazing use of brute force in a special-purpose way that didn’t generalize to all that much else. 

The market seems to get all of this - RH hasn’t moved $ANT much after hours – even if a lot of people here don’t.

Paraphrasing something I said here yesterday, clinging to the Riemann results like a life raft after the stock market correction doesn’t change the fact that (a) current AI still isn’t trustworthy enough to for many applications and (b) is still not profitable enough to warrant the massive investments.

In 2006, Apple asked Intel to build the chip for the first iPhone.

Intel's team ran the cost numbers.

In September 2014, Apple moved its flagship A8 iPhone chip orders to TSMC on its 20nm line.

What The Chip Happened To AI Stock Investors Today (NEWS EVEN ON THE WEEKEND)!!

SK Hynix
$SKHY
The weekend's wildest headline came from memory. The Information reported Friday night that SoftBank's Masayoshi Son approached Wall Street institutions about financing a buyout of SK Hynix worth roughly $1 trillion. SoftBank didn't deny it, saying only that the idea is "no longer under active consideration," and SK Hynix said it had no knowledge of the matter and that any foreign takeover needs Korean government approval. The deal itself is reported, the statements are confirmed. What it really shows is how strategic HBM has become: Son owns pieces of almost every layer of AI except memory. The open question is whether anyone else starts thinking about memory this way.

Samsung
$SSNLF
Samsung's memory story kept tightening even as chip stocks sold off. Korean outlet Economy Tribune reported Saturday, citing a person familiar with the matter, that most of Samsung's memory capacity through 2029 is already booked, with some customers asking for supply guarantees that stretch into the next decade. That part is a report. What is confirmed comes from Samsung's own Q3 call, where it said long term deals were signed with 10 customers, more are in negotiation, and the contracts carry price floors. Put that next to Micron's sold out comments on Friday and the memory makers are all telling the same story. The caveat is that contracts only matter if customers can keep paying.

TSMC
$TSM
Taiwan stepped in after its market had its worst week in decades. The Taiex fell more than 6% on Friday and about 17.5% for the week, and on Saturday the Financial Supervisory Commission confirmed a blanket ban on short selling below the previous close starting Monday, the first since 2015. It also raised short selling margin requirements, paused new put warrant listings and encouraged buybacks. This is confirmed by the regulator. For AI investors, Taiwan is the supply chain, and TSMC dominates the index, so this is a government trying to stop forced selling in its most important asset. The open question is whether bans calm the market or just delay the selling.

Amazon
$AMZN
Amazon may be about to spend real money on the chip war with Nvidia. The Financial Times reported Saturday that Amazon is in advanced talks to buy AI startup Decart for about $7.5 billion, with a deal possibly announced as early as next week. Decart's software helps AI models run efficiently across different chips, and it was an early showcase customer for Amazon's Trainium. Neither company has confirmed anything, so treat this as a report. If it closes, Amazon is buying a tool that makes moving workloads off Nvidia GPUs easier, which fits the custom silicon theme. The caveat is the price, roughly double the valuation Decart raised at in May.

SpaceX
$SPCX
Elon Musk added a sober note to the AI financing debate. In a post on X Saturday, he wrote that getting this much compute "turned on, cooled and working reliably is incredibly hard," and that "the cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year." His point is that even a few months of delay between paying for compute and earning revenue from it means hundreds of billions of extra working capital across the industry. These are his own words, not a report. It lands right after SpaceX's giant GPU financing, and it echoes the credit worries hitting neoclouds. The open question is who funds that gap if markets stay shut.

posts.text:
Buy when the VIX spikes, not when the headlines clear

A sharp rise in the VIX has repeatedly been followed by solid equity returns. The pattern is clear enough that it is worth revisiting after the latest episode.

On 20 November the VIX jumped 9.29 points to 37.73. The S&P 500 fell 3.43 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 5.95 per cent. Since the start of 1996 there have been 90 sessions in which the VIX rose by more than five points in a single day. 

In the periods that followed those days, the median forward return for the S&P 500 was 5.62 per cent over three months, 10.86 per cent over six months and 19.87 per cent over one year. The Nasdaq 100 recorded corresponding median gains of 8.40 per cent, 16.66 per cent and 31.14 per cent. Returns are measured from the close on the day of the spike.

The current volatility term structure reinforces the contrary signal. Spot VIX is above the levels priced three and six months ahead, indicating that investors are paying a premium for near-term protection. Fear is concentrated in the present.

A violent sell-off changes quoted prices immediately. It does not erase the customers, competitive positions or cash-generation capacity of sound businesses. The practical implication is selective: quality and diversified equity exposure have historically been the assets that recovered most reliably once the immediate panic subsided.

Markets rarely present attractive entry points under calm headlines. The more common setting is falling prices and elevated demand for protection. The historical record after large daily VIX increases shows that those moments have, on average, rewarded investors who were prepared to act while others were still focused on the risks that had already materialised.

In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

In July, Christopher Cox, chairman of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, announced a plan to curb improper (naked) short-selling. In doing so he has (de facto) attempted to limit the activity of short-sellers. Mr Cox seems to be implicitly blaming the shorts for the unprecedented fall of bank, ­government-sponsored agency and brokerage stocks over the past year – even though short-sellers were the very group that warned of the dangerous credit cycle and its consequences.

Short-selling runs deep in financial history. Perhaps the first case dates to 1609 when the Dutch trader, Isaac Le Maire, targeted the shares of the shipping company Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie (the Dutch East India Company). VOC was the first multinational corporation in history and had broad powers. Nonetheless, Le Maire, concerned about threats of attack by English ships, sold VOC’s shares short. After learning about Le Maire’s tactics, the stock exchange governing VOC’s trading banned short-selling (although the ban was later revoked). In the early 1630s, the Dutch economy fell into a depression following a speculative peak in the trading of tulips.

Again, short-selling raised the ire of regulators, many of whom saw it as magnifying the effect on the Dutch economic downturn. As a result, England banned short-selling outright. Almost 420 years later – in the late 1920s – short-sellers warned of the consequences of speculation. But in the aftermath of the Wall Street crash of 1929, many blamed them and the uptick rule – which banned short-selling on downticks – was instituted (and stayed in effect until 2007).

More regulation governing short-selling came into force in 1940, with a ban on mutual funds from short-selling (though that law was lifted in 1997). In early 2005, the SEC again sought to restrict the practice. Yet short-sellers have served as financial watchdogs, as many of their warnings have been spot on. The delusional dotcom boom in the late 1990s brought Cassandra-like utterings from the short-selling cabal that proved insightful but were largely ignored.

After the subsequent 75 per cent collapse of the Nasdaq, a bull market in corporate fraud emerged and short-sellers such as David Rocker, founder of Rocker Partners, highlighted accounting problems at companies such as Sunbeam, Tyco and Lernout & Hauspie. We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions.

STOP 🛑 calling this an AI bubble 

In March 2000, at the peak of the dot-com bubble, leading technology stocks traded at extremely high price-to-sales (P/S) ratios. Cisco reached roughly 37x trailing sales, while Microsoft and Oracle traded around 26x. Investors were pricing in years of perfect, uninterrupted growth for internet infrastructure and software companies many of which were not yet highly profitable.

By contrast, in late 2026 the major AI-related stocks are trading at far lower multiples. NVIDIA sits around 8.7x trailing sales (roughly 6.5-7.5x on forward estimates), Microsoft around 10.5× trailing (about 9x forward), and Alphabet near 7× trailing (closer to 5.5-6.5x forward). Even after strong multi-year runs, these companies are valued at a fraction of the 2000 peaks.

The gap is striking because today’s large AI names are already highly profitable, generate substantial cash flow, and have demonstrated real product demand, whereas many 2000 era leaders were still early in monetizing the internet. While elevated AI capital spending introduces some uncertainty, the current multiples show that investors are not pricing these stocks anywhere near the extreme optimism of the 2000 bubble.

Some random, unfiltered thoughts on AI and the market:

The gulf between “San Francisco” and “New York” has never been wider than it is right now 

AI is accelerating in capability, rapidly and in a way that is structurally changing, and in many ways upending, the nature of the firm and the fundamentals of capitalism

If that sounds extreme, consider that Anthropic has ~6,000 employees, Meta has 67,000, and both companies are worth ~$1.5T

Talk to your average startup and it’s clear that, given the opportunity to start from scratch, nobody is building their companies “the old way.” 

Talk to your average Fortune 500 company and it’s clear that getting an AI agent into production at scale is a Herculean task

Intelligence may not be the bottleneck, but firms built from the foundational assumption that intelligence is improving quickly in capability and price are scaling at a genuinely unbelievably velocity

There’s a reason Zuck wanted to fire 60% of many of the teams at his company, in large part likely out of frustration that he can’t start from scratch like his competitors had the luxury of doing

A structurally weaker Nvidia and OpenAI have minimal impact on the pace and impact of AI diffusing across the economy (“San Francisco”), but completely breaks the models built in “New York.” Hence the absolute freak-out these last few weeks. It was all priced to go perfectly and now things are not perfect 

But for the boots on the ground, AI will not slow down. And counterintuitively, economic weakness might accelerate diffusion. After all, tokens are much more fungible and flexible than people

Where does that leave us? I think firmly in the second phase of the AI build-out. Real value is being built in the app layer (though how defensible it is…TBD).  

Trying to predict the next bottleneck, or whether Washington does this or that other thing wrt policy, or exactly how many data centers get built out…who can say? Certainly not me. It’s not the bet I’m trying to make 

I’m looking at who wins from rapidly improving intelligence available at increasingly cheaper prices, and critically, which leaders are able to move with conviction into this new operating paradigm

Commodities are getting hit pretty hard alongside the broader equity market as the surging U.S. dollar sucks liquidity out of the global financial system.  For those that follow me, I've been saying this from some time that there was risks if the dollar strengthens too quickly. 

The issue is that dollar-denominated debt becomes more expensive to service, financial conditions tighten, and investors are forced to raise cash, reduce leverage and sell assets. It becomes less about fundamentals and more about liquidity.

One thing I've learned over the years is that market leverage doesn't necessarily tell you when a correction will happen, but it tells you a great deal about how painful that correction could become. That's an extraordinary amount of leverage in the system, and when markets start moving against investors, it can accelerate the selling pressure.

URANIUM'S BIGGEST PROBLEM: THE MINES THAT DON'T EXIST YET

Utilities are covered today. But who supplies their reactors in 2030, 2032 or 2035?

That's the tension in a December 2025 interview with Justin Huhn of Uranium Insider. The argument is even more relevant today.

In the 2000s uranium boom, spot went from below $10 to about $135/lb. Some mining shares rose 10- to 100-fold before crashing.

Huhn believes this cycle could last longer because uranium supply responds painfully slowly to higher prices.

A deposit cannot become a mine just because spot reaches $100. It needs permits, financing, infrastructure, construction and a successful ramp-up. That takes years.

Demand is more predictable. Reactors need refuelling, life extensions add consumption, and Japan is restarting units. China is building reactors, buying overseas uranium and expanding fuel services. Data centres add another reason to preserve nuclear power.

THE CONTRACTING CLOCK IS TICKING

Utilities are comfortable near term. Further out, the picture changes dramatically.

Sprott, citing U.S. EIA data, estimates maximum U.S. utility contract coverage falls from about 98% in 2026 to 60% in 2030 and just 9% by 2033.

That isn't a fuel-shortage forecast. Utilities can sign contracts and draw inventories.

But it means substantial demand remains unsecured, just as the market is counting on mines that have yet to produce a pound.

CAMECO IS SHOWING ITS HAND

Huhn's interview quoted $75/lb spot and $86/lb long-term. Those figures are dated.

On November 20, spot was around $90/lb. TradeTech's October long-term indicator hit $99/lb.

More revealing is what Cameco says about contracts.

In its Q3 2026 call, Cameco described market-linked floors in the mid-to-high $70s, ceilings reaching $160, and three-digit prices on fixed-price portions.

These are contract terms, not a guarantee of $160 realized prices. But they show how much bargaining power disciplined producers have gained.

Huhn argues new major mines need sustained higher prices, potentially north of $100/lb, to justify financing and execution risk.

A short spike won't build a mine. Sustained incentive pricing might.

THE MINES THAT MUST DELIVER

NexGen's Arrow study forecasts 28.8 million lb a year for its first five years. Enormous supply from one mine.

Since Huhn spoke, NexGen secured its construction licence in March 2026 and started construction in June.

But construction isn't production. Shaft sinking, ground conditions, commissioning and ramp-up still matter. NexGen's own capital-cost estimate has already risen from about C$1.3 billion in its 2021 study to C$2.2 billion in a 2024 update.

And Arrow is only one mine. Future supply depends on other projects delivering as promised.

If they slip, utilities can't order replacement pounds from mines that don't exist.

THE FINANCIAL WILDCARD

Huhn also explains the carry trade: when forward uranium prices sufficiently exceed spot, traders can buy uranium, store it and sell it for future delivery.

That can support spot buying before utilities need delivery. It is not a guaranteed price floor.

Physical trusts and speculative traders could amplify a rally. They could amplify the downside too.

MY JUDGMENT

Huhn sees opportunities in beaten-down small uranium stocks. Perhaps. But this is where I'd be selective.

A shortage doesn't make every deposit profitable. Higher uranium prices won't fix bad contracts, excessive capex, weak management or repeated dilution.

Some stocks gained 1,000% or more in the last bull market. Others never rewarded shareholders.

The opportunity isn't simply to own uranium in the ground.

It's to own companies that turn it into profitable pounds before shareholders run out of patience and money.

Buy when there is blood in the streets! 

Extreme fear is setting up the next leg higher

The S&P 500 has fallen 11.6% from its October high in seven straight sessions. Friday’s close sat 4.1 standard deviations below the 50-day average, the most oversold reading since August 2015. The Arms Index posted back-to-back capitulation readings. This is what extreme fear looks like, and extreme fear has historically marked buying opportunities, not the start of bear markets.

The market closed the week at 6,910, right on 6,900, the key Fibonacci support level of this year’s rally. Fast V-shaped recoveries form within days of capitulation, and corrections that hold support don’t become bear markets. From 6,900, the strongest past fast-V recoveries delivered 12-month gains of up to 38%, which puts 9,500 within reach. The timing adds to the case. 

The market is entering the sweet spot of the four-year presidential cycle, and the S&P has been higher a year after every midterm election since 1950.

Add a Fed pivot, and 10,000 is still in play. S&P 500 earnings will reach $450 in 2027, so the only argument is over the multiple. With the energy crisis passing, the 10-year Treasury yield will head to 4%, and the Greenspan Fed model then implies a multiple of 25. 

Even 22 times earnings gets the index to 10,000. Nothing has changed except the level of fear. There is no recession and no financial crisis, and investors will come to see AI not as a three-year buildout but as something like the railroads.

Fear flips to greed, as it did in 1998. After the Asian currency crisis and the Russia and LTCM shock, the S&P 500 fell 19% from its July peak. The Fed cut three times, the index regained its high by late November, and a year after the October low it was up 39%. When the Fed has eased after a no-recession sell-off, as in 1998, 2019 and 2025, the median 12-month gain has been 33.7%.

Many cite the 1990s to argue that the supply of AI capacity is outstripping demand. That’s wrong. The real lesson of the 1990s is the one Alan Greenspan drew: productivity gains let an economy run hot without stoking inflation. In 1995, after the Fed pivoted from hiking to easing with no recession, the S&P 500 gained 34.1%, the best pre-election year since 1950.

Leveraged products now amplify every swing between fear and greed, and this week’s selling was fear at full volume. The old saying is to buy when there is blood in the streets. Today there is no recession and no financial crisis, the energy shock is ending, and productivity and earnings are growing strongly. A Fed pivot is coming, and the market is cheap. 

That’s the time to buy.

Everyone is scratching his head after the recent market sell-off, but it’s really not that complicated. It’s pure math. Let’s take a look, shall we?

At their peaks, the major listed AI-exposed companies (Mag7 plus key chip, foundry, and infrastructure names) were worth roughly $28–32 trillion. Add Anthropic’s post-IPO valuation of about $1.2–1.5 trillion and an expected OpenAI post-IPO figure around $1.5 trillion, and the total sits in the $30–35 trillion range, approaching half the entire US equity market (recently ~$70–72 trillion).

Once a single theme absorbed that much capital, further large gains required either massive new inflows or more money pulled from everything else. At some point neither was available at the necessary scale. Expecting these names to double again from those peaks implied an incremental $30+ trillion of market value. The rest of the US market was only ~$40 trillion; global equity markets, bonds, and private capital held no unused liquidity of that magnitude ready for AI multiples. Leverage, retail flows, and foreign capital were already heavily committed.

The arithmetic simply stopped working. Prices could no longer be justified by any realistic path of further capital absorption. The pullback was the delayed recognition that the liquidity sucked into the trade had nowhere left to come from. It’s really that simple. Seriously, what were people thinking buying these names at multi-trillion valuations? That they would double again in three months?

posts.name: Antonio García Martínez
posts.text:
Watched 'Sirat' on @tylercowen's recommendation as best film of 2026.

It's spectacular. The amateur actors made me think of all the nomadic counterculture types I met backpacking around Europe in the 90s (now a bit old and grizzled and past their peak rave days, but still wandering).

The cinematography was a motion-picture landscape painting. 

The not-so-subtle political commentary on how these supposed bohemians are just obnoxious tourists somehow delusionally entering a conflict-zone the locals are trying to escape (and eventually paying for it).

The drug-fueled nihilism of it all, with human connection somehow surviving the LSD trips and endless hours inside rundown campers.

The easy manner they switch between French and Spanish until it becomes one patois, like anyone who's drifted between the two countries often. 

A bit long, but you have to settle into the rhythm of it. Unique film. 

Per the Quranic reference of the title, the supposed paradise they're seeking in the desert turns into hell very quickly. An American version of this would be some rah-rah Burning Man bore...the Euro version is a lot darker and more interesting.
